headline: Scientists Confirm First-Ever Moon Beyond Our Solar System
meta_description: Astronomers detect the first confirmed exosatellite orbiting a brown dwarf in the CD-35 2722 star system, reshaping how we understand moons across the universe.
summary_short: A groundbreaking discovery in Chile reveals what may be the universe's first confirmed moon outside our solar system—but it's nothing like ours.
body:
For decades, astronomers have searched the cosmos for moons beyond Earth's neighborhood, but until now, none had been confidently detected. That changed when Kevin Hoy, an ESO student in Chile, and his team used the Very Large Telescope to identify what appears to be the first confirmed exosatellite in the CD-35 2722 star system. The discovery is remarkable not just for being a first, but for challenging everything we thought we knew about what a moon actually is. Unlike the small, rocky moons orbiting planets in our solar system, this newly found object is roughly the size of Jupiter and doesn't orbit a planet—it orbits a brown dwarf, which itself orbits a star. "This system is somewhat hard to define using Solar-System-based words," Hoy acknowledged, noting the discovery as "super weird" compared to our own cosmic neighborhood.

The team used a technique called the radial velocity method—the same approach that detected the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star—to spot the tiny wobbles in the brown dwarf caused by the gravity of its orbiting companion. The evidence they gathered is compelling enough that Alice Zurlo, director of YEMS, a multidisciplinary research center focused on detecting exoplanets and exomoons, called it "the first plausible detection of an exosatellite."

If confirmed, this breakthrough could accelerate the hunt for similar worlds across the universe. Since six of the eight planets in our solar system have natural moons, scientists reasoned they should be fairly common everywhere—the challenge has always been their small size relative to what they orbit. Now that astronomers know where to look and how to find them, the age of exomoon discovery may finally be beginning.
quick_facts: First confirmed exosatellite detected in CD-35 2722 star system
Kevin Hoy led study using ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile
The exosatellite is roughly Jupiter-sized, orbiting a brown dwarf
Only a few exomoon candidates spotted before this discovery
